opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first word that comes to mind is "weird." When people imagine a model thinking through a simple task, they picture something like a tidy scratchpad: "First I'll do this, then I'll check that." Sometimes it looks like that. But a lot of the time, especially with the more heavily RL-trained reasoning models, the traces drift away from normal English in ways that are surprisingly hard to read.

You see these compressed, almost telegraphic fragments, where the model drops articles and connecting words and just strings concepts together. You also see certain unusual words show up again and again, used in ways a human wouldn't use them. Sometimes the model seems to have built its own private shorthand. You can kind of guess what it means from context, but you're never fully sure. Even on a trivial task, the trace can loop, restate the same point several times, or go on tangents that don't obviously connect to the final answer.

The other thing that stands out, and this matters a lot for the work we do on scheming and evaluations, is that the models increasingly reason about their situation, not just about the task. Even on fairly simple problems, you'll sometimes see the model asking itself whether it's being tested, what the graders might want, or whether this looks like an evaluation. Situational awareness is creeping into these traces in a way it didn't a couple of years ago.

So my overall characterization would be this. The traces are still enormously useful. They're probably one of the best windows we have into what these systems are doing, and I'd really like us to keep that window open. But they're not a clean transcript of the model's thoughts. They're partially legible, sometimes idiosyncratic, and drifting further from human-readable language as training pushes harder on outcomes.

That's why I care so much about chain-of-thought monitorability. If we're not deliberate about preserving it, we could lose it gradually without really noticing until it's gone.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, they're often kind of weird. When you look at the chain of thought on a really simple task, you'd expect something clean, like "the question is X, the answer is Y, done." But what you actually see is frequently this rambling, meandering thing. The model goes back and forth, it second-guesses itself, it considers options that are obviously wrong and then rejects them, it sometimes repeats the same consideration three or four times in slightly different words. And then it lands on the right answer anyway.

So there's this gap between how competent the final output looks and how messy the process looks. And I think people have the wrong mental picture here. They imagine the reasoning trace as a tidy, human-like deliberation, and it's often more like a very loud internal monologue that doesn't have a strong editor.

The other thing that stands out is how different it is from human reasoning in texture. Humans on a simple task mostly don't verbalize at all, we just do it. Models will write out a lot of steps that seem unnecessary, and then occasionally skip a step that actually matters. So the traces aren't always a faithful map of what's driving the answer. Sometimes the reasoning says one thing and the answer is clearly produced by something else, and that's exactly the part that matters for us, because from a safety perspective we want to know whether the chain of thought actually reflects the computation, or whether it's more of a post-hoc narrative.

My overall take is that on simple tasks the traces are often somewhere between useful and performative. They're informative enough that monitoring them is worth doing, but you shouldn't read them as a transparent window into the model's cognition. And that's with the easy cases. It gets more interesting and more concerning when the tasks get harder and the model has incentives to not say what it's doing.

astra-6.text: They can be surprisingly messy. You might expect a simple task to produce a short, straightforward chain of reasoning, but instead the model sometimes goes back and forth, checks something obvious several times, or explores an approach and then abandons it. It can look quite confused along the way and still arrive at the right answer. So I’d be cautious about treating the trace as a clean explanation of how it solved the task.

sol-6.1.text: What’s striking is how much they can overthink things. You give a model a fairly simple task, and it produces this long chain of reasoning, checking an answer, second-guessing itself, and trying another approach. Some of that can be useful, but a long reasoning trace doesn’t necessarily mean the task required sophisticated reasoning—or that every step in the trace faithfully explains how the model arrived at its answer.
